claims.statement: In adults with alcohol dependence in double-blind outpatient trials, most of them European and most after detoxification, acamprosate compared with placebo is associated with fewer people returning to any drinking during treatment: across 16 trials pooled in a review for the US Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality, 1,968 of 2,576 people on acamprosate (76 in 100) and 1,893 of 2,271 on placebo (83 in 100) drank again (crude totals, editors' arithmetic), a pooled difference of 9 in 100 (risk difference −0.09, 95% CI −0.14 to −0.04; 12 people treated for one to benefit), with large differences between trials (I² 80.8%) (Jonas et al., 2014; funded by the agency; no conflicts declared); its 2023 update gives a risk ratio of 0.88 (0.83 to 0.93; 20 trials, 6,380 people) and a Cochrane review 0.86 (0.81 to 0.91; 24 trials) (McPheeters et al., 2023; Rösner et al., 2010). In the Cochrane review abstinent days rose by about 11 in every 100 days (10.94 percentage points, 5.08 to 16.81; I² 94%), and in 7 trials fewer people on acamprosate had returned to drinking 3 to 12 months after treatment ended (risk ratio 0.91, 0.87 to 0.96). Acamprosate did not reduce return to heavy drinking (risk ratio 0.99, 0.94 to 1.05; 7 trials). In the 4 trials at low risk of bias the difference was not clear (risk difference −0.02, −0.09 to 0.05); the two of them with by far the most events, both in the US and one of them COMBINE, found no benefit, while most of the other 15 trials were European and recruited from inpatient settings or treatment programmes. The 2014 authors list population differences, other heterogeneity, chance or 'no true association between acamprosate and return to drinking' as possible explanations. Of the Cochrane review's 24 trials, 17 were run or supported by drug companies, mostly the manufacturer, though industry-run and non-profit trials gave similar estimates (risk ratios 0.88 and 0.88). Diarrhoea was more common (11 more in 100; risk difference 0.11, 0.09 to 0.13), and more people stopped because of side effects (risk ratio 1.35, 1.01 to 1.80). Head to head, acamprosate and naltrexone did not differ (return to any drinking risk ratio 1.03, 0.96 to 1.10; 3 trials). The three reviews share most of their trials. Certainty: low. Status: mixed.
claims.magnitude: Jonas et al. 2014 (against placebo, trials at low or medium risk of bias): return to any drinking RD −0.09 (95% CI −0.14 to −0.04), 16 trials, 4847, I² 80.8%, NNT 12 (8 to 26), moderate strength of evidence; crude totals 1968/2576 (76.4%) against 1893/2271 (83.4%) (editors' arithmetic from Figure 2); by risk of bias, post hoc: high or unclear −0.13 (−0.20 to −0.06), 3 trials, 757; medium −0.11 (−0.16 to −0.06), 12 trials, 3438; low −0.02 (−0.09 to 0.05), 4 trials, 1409; return to heavy drinking −0.01 (−0.04 to 0.03), 7 trials, 2496; percentage of drinking days WMD −8.8 (−12.8 to −4.8), 13 trials; deaths 7 against 6 (8 trials, 2677), insufficient. McPheeters et al. 2023: return to any drinking RR 0.88 (0.83 to 0.93), 20 trials, 6380, moderate (I² 77.6%); return to heavy drinking 0.99 (0.94 to 1.05), 7 trials, moderate (no effect); percentage of drinking days −8.3 (−12.2 to −4.4), 14 trials; diarrhoea RR 1.58 (1.27 to 1.97). Rösner et al. 2010 (Cochrane): return to any drinking RR 0.86 (0.81 to 0.91), 24 trials, 6172, NNTB 9.09 (6.66 to 14.28); abstinent days MD 10.94 percentage points (5.08 to 16.81), 19 trials, I² 94%; after treatment RR 0.91 (0.87 to 0.96), 7 trials, 1986; return to heavy drinking 0.99 (0.94 to 1.04), 6 trials, 2132; diarrhoea RD 0.11 (0.09 to 0.13), 16 trials; drop-out because of adverse events RR 1.35 (1.01 to 1.80), 19 trials; by funding, fully industry-sponsored 0.88 (0.80 to 0.97), 11 trials, partly industry-supported 0.84 (0.78 to 0.89), 6 trials, non-profit 0.88 (0.81 to 0.96), 7 trials. COMBINE: acamprosate main effect on percent days abstinent 78.4 against 77.6 (P=.61); time to first heavy drinking day HR 0.85 (0.63 to 1.15), the paper's main-effect hazard ratio, whose basis is unclear (study card sc_anton_2006).
